content: SIM2, or Single-minded homolog 2, is a protein in humans encoded by the SIM2 gene. This protein is critically involved in the development of the central nervous system midline and the formation of facial and cranial structures. Function The SIM1 and SIM2 genes are homologs of the Drosophila single-minded (sim) gene. In Drosophila, the sim gene encodes a transcription factor that serves as a master regulator of neurogenesis in midline cells of the central nervous system. Based on its chromosomal location, its role as a transcriptional repressor, and its similarity to the Drosophila sim gene, it has been hypothesized that SIM2 may contribute to specific phenotypes observed in Down syndrome. Interactions SIM2 has been shown to interact with the aryl hydrocarbon receptor nuclear translocator (ARNT). When the SIM2 gene is transfected into PC12 cells, it disrupts the normal cycle of cell maturation. Specifically, SIM2 inhibits the expression of cyclin E, which prevents cells from progressing through the G1/S checkpoint of the cell cycle, thereby suppressing cellular proliferation. Additionally, SIM2 upregulates the expression of p27, a protein that inhibits growth. The presence of p27 further suppresses the activation of cell cycle regulatory kinases. Disease State The SIM2 gene can exist in three states: +/+, +/-, and -/-. When the gene is expressed as SIM2 -/-, it is considered disrupted, leading to numerous physical malformations, particularly in the craniofacial region. Individuals with SIM2 -/exhibit either complete or partial clefting of the secondary palate, as well as malformations of the tongue and the pterygoid processes of the sphenoid bone. These abnormalities result in aerophagia (swallowing of air), which can lead to postnatal death. Severe aerophagia causes air accumulation in the gastrointestinal tract, leading to abdominal distension. Overexpression of the SIM2 gene is thought to contribute to some of the phenotypic deformities characteristic of Down syndrome. SIM2 mRNA has been detected in various regions of the brain that exhibit abnormalities in individuals with Down syndrome, as well as in the palate, oral and tongue epithelia, mandibular and hyoid bones. SIM2 Short (SIM2s) There are two known isoforms of SIM2, each playing distinct roles in different tissues. The SIM2 Short (SIM2s) isoform is specifically expressed in mammary gland tissue. SIM2s is a splice variant that lacks exon 11 of the SIM2 gene. Research has shown that SIM2s is involved in mammary gland development and exhibits tumor-suppressive properties, particularly in breast cancer. In mouse models, the absence of SIM2s expression in mammary epithelial cells results in developmental defects that resemble cancer-like characteristics. These defects include increased cell proliferation, invasion of local stroma, loss of cellular polarity, and loss of E-cadherin, a key cell adhesion molecule. These findings suggest that SIM2s is essential for proper mammary gland development. Experiments reintroducing SIM2s into human breast cancer cells have demonstrated its tumor-suppressive effects. Immunohistochemical staining has shown that SIM2s is more highly expressed in normal human breast cells compared to cancerous ones. Reintroducing SIM2s expression in breast cancer cells results in decreased growth, proliferation, and invasiveness. SIM2s represses the activity of the matrix metalloprotease-3 (MMP3) gene, which is involved in cell migration, cancer progression, and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transitions (EMT). SIM2s also suppresses the SLUG transcription factor, which in turn inhibits EMT. By suppressing EMT, SIM2s allows E-cadherin to remain intact, preventing pathological EMT associated with tumor formation. These actions highlight the tumor-suppressive role of SIM2s in mammary epithelium. Knockout Model Scientists can intentionally knock out or disrupt the SIM2 gene using homologous recombination. This process involves eliminating the predicted start codon and the subsequent 47 amino acids. An EcoRI restriction site is then introduced into the chromosome.
